summary: Describes how RFCs are published. The definitive version moved from plain text to XML using RFCXML, and different publication versions are rendered from it. It obsoletes RFC 7990 and updates the status of earlier documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9720 explains how one definitive RFCXML file relates to the HTML, plain-text, and PDF versions people read. It permits reissues to correct the source or keep presentation consistent, while requiring the intended meaning to be preserved as much as possible. Earlier versions are archived.

subtitle: How RFCXML, published versions, reissues, and archives fit together.

tldr.problem: RFC 7990 used the term canonical for both a source format and an authoritative version. Publishing experience also showed that RFCXML sometimes needs correction after an RFC is published.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9720 distinguishes the definitive format and version from publication formats and versions. It allows the RFC Production Center to reissue documents while preserving their semantic content and archiving earlier versions.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7990, updates RFC 9280, and has itself been updated by RFC 9920.

today: RFC 9720 is Informational. It obsoletes RFC 7990, updates RFC 9280, and has itself been updated by RFC 9920.

sections.title: Why the Publication Rules Changed
sections.content:
RFC 7990 described an XML-based process for creating RFC publication formats. Experience with published RFCXML showed that an RFC's XML file may need narrowly limited changes, and that the word canonical had been used for two different concepts.

RFC 9720 concerns producing published RFCs, not how individual streams develop and review Internet-Drafts. It replaces the older terminology and says the production details may continue to change as the community and the RFC Production Center gain experience.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier rules used one word for both the source file and the published copy. This RFC gives those ideas separate names and updates the publication process.

sections.title: Four Terms for RFC Formats and Versions
sections.content:
The definitive format is RFCXML, and the definitive version is a published RFC in that format. A publication format is currently HTML, plain text, or PDF; a publication version is the RFC rendered in one of those formats.

The RFC also renames “xml2rfc version 3” as RFCXML and calls the publishing body the RFC Production Center (RPC). These terms distinguish the source from the versions produced for readers.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCXML is the definitive format. HTML, plain text, and PDF are publication formats made from it.

sections.title: The Definitive Version
sections.content:
The RPC's final RFCXML file contains the information intended for the RFC and is self-contained for rendering its publication versions. The RPC may update it for reasons such as schema changes, XML errors, or changes to publication tools.

Any changes must preserve the semantics expressed in the original RFC. The RPC keeps a public record of reissues and gives a short reason for each change. The document allows risk to be assessed and mitigated rather than requiring every possibility of semantic change to be eliminated.
sections.plainLanguage: The definitive version is the complete source for the published RFC. It can be corrected, but the RPC must preserve the original meaning and record why it made a change.

sections.title: Publication Versions and Archives
sections.content:
The RPC may reissue publication versions, but it is not required to do so. It considers both the risk of changing meaning and the consistency of the RFC Series. A changed XML file can lead to publication versions being regenerated, even when readers see no difference.

The RPC archives definitive versions and previously published publication versions. Archived versions must be available through the same access methods as current versions, and each archive records when its version was created or reissued.
sections.plainLanguage: The RPC can publish a revised rendering when appropriate and keeps earlier versions available. Each archived version records when it was created or reissued.

sections.title: The Updated Stability Policy
sections.content:
RFC 9280 previously said that published RFC Series documents are not changed. RFC 9720 replaces that rule: RFCs may be reissued, while the semantic content of publication versions should be preserved to the greatest extent possible.

The update also permits reissues to maintain a consistent presentation. The RPC is expected to identify, track, and actively mitigate the risks of unintended changes during editing or regeneration.
sections.plainLanguage: A published RFC may now be reissued. The new version should preserve what the original says, and the RPC must manage the risks of making a change.
